post.summary: Change the admin password.

Requires the current password. Answers **204** on success; every session
but the acting one is dropped. A wrong current password is **401**, and a
new password below the length floor is **422**.

post.summary: Set a transient root password.
post.description:
The password must be 8 to 72 bytes and contain no NUL, newline or carriage
return. 72 is bcrypt's limit — a longer password would be silently
truncated, so it is refused instead.

The password is written into no setting, is never logged, and lasts until
the next reboot. A **422** states which bound was broken and never repeats
the password back.

Answers **202** once the password hash is written and its scoped apply is queued.

post.summary: Rotate a WireGuard interface's private key.
post.description:
An action rather than a settings write: the private key lives in a
mode-0640 file on STATE that the settings tree does not describe. micad
draws a new key, tears down the device holding the old one and reconciles.

Answers **200** with the new public key — the tunnel is already running on
it. The private half is never returned. **404** when `iface` names no
declared `network` entry; **422** when the entry exists but is not of kind
`wireguard`.

**The trust list is not here.** Devices arrive by pairing and leave by
being removed; a route that replaced the whole list would let a client
declare a device it never paired with, which the adapter would then have
no keys for. Nor is discoverability, the name or a pairing code: the
adapter is discoverable only while a pairing window is open, advertises
the hostname, and offers no fixed code.

Served only when the product carries the `bluetooth` feature (`GET /api/v1/meta` lists `features`); otherwise every method answers 404 `not_found`.

get.summary:
Report how this device was claimed and whether its credential must still be
rotated.
get.description:
**Authenticated, deliberately.** `GET /api/v1/session` already tells an
unauthenticated caller whether the device is in setup mode, and that is all
an unauthenticated caller learns here too — "this device was claimed from a
medium and is still holding the password that was on it" is a sentence an
attacker would act on, and the operator who needs to read it is signed in
by construction.

This is the surface that makes the bound observable BEFORE it bites: the
operator who claimed a device with a provisioning document sees
`rotationRequired` here, and can see it the moment they sign in rather than
on the first mutation the device turns away.

post.summary: Recover the management credential: rotate, never reveal.
post.description:
**Presence is the authority, and the only one.** An authenticated
management session may NOT run this flow — a session that can rotate the
credential it authenticated with is a session-fixation lever, and an
operator holding a working credential needs
`POST /api/v1/actions/change-password` rather than recovery. So the route
takes no credential extractor and refuses a caller that presents one.

**What it does, in order.** It MINTS a new password — it never
discloses, decrypts or derives the previous secret, and there is no code
path from here to a stored plaintext. It publishes the new one exactly
once, on the channel that proved presence. Only then does it commit, in ONE
write of `access`: the new hash, the emptied token list, the claim record
and the bumped generation together. Publishing first is the safe
direction — a crash between the two must not be a self-inflicted lockout —
so the worst outcome here is a credential the operator saw and that never
worked, which the flow being cheap to re-run answers.

**The previous credential stops working at that commit**, and so does every
API token: "any client or automation holding it must
be re-enrolled". Every session goes with it, for the reason a password
change drops them.

**A device claimed by a provisioning document.** Its
bootstrap secret sat in plaintext on a medium, and losing it before the
forced rotation is a recovery case rather than a claim case. A recovery writes the claim record with the channel that claimed the
device preserved and `rotationRequired` FALSE: the credential this flow
mints was drawn by the device from the system CSPRNG and shown once at the device, so
it is not a bootstrap secret, and demanding a rotation of a credential that
was just rotated under physical presence would be a bound with nothing left
to protect.

**An unclaimed device is refused**, pointing at `POST /api/v1/setup`. There
is nothing to recover on a device that has no credential, and minting one
here would be another channel that can claim a device —
`micad_settings::ClaimChannel` names every one and says why.

**One rotation per presence assertion**. The assertion is read and
spent inside one guard, so a second request — concurrent, or later inside

**This route stages; micad applies.** A reset is an intent
record plus an idempotent apply, so the whole of this handler's write is

leaves the device either not asked or asked, never half-reset. micad carries
the tier out before anything else on the next boot and clears the record.

`ResetTier` has two members, so `secure-wipe` is a body this route cannot
parse, and `full-factory` is answered with the route that erases the
device, `POST /api/v1/system/factory-reset`.

A tier staged over another replaces it. Both are audited, so nothing is
silent, and the alternative — refusing until something un-stages the first
— is a dead end for an operator who asked for the wrong one.

about the clock — a device nobody could query is not a device that was
queried and found out of sync — so the `synchronized` member is absent
there and `detail` names the read that went missing. Read-only: there is
no route that pauses or stops synchronization.

post.summary: Write the operator's update configuration.
post.description:
The one route that changes what this device does on its own: which address
it dials, whether it checks, fetches and installs
unattended, and inside which maintenance window. It takes the same
administrator authority every other management write takes, and there is no
unauthenticated or fleet-derived path to it.

**apid does not write the file.** micad owns `/mica/config/updates.json` and
is its only writer; this route asks. The validation is therefore the same
code the update subsystem reads the document with, so a document that is
accepted here is one that loads, and a rejected one is refused with the
offending field named **before** anything is replaced. `auto` with no
maintenance window is refused here rather than failing closed some hours
later at a check the operator would have to go looking for.

**POST**, because it puts the radio to work: a scan sweeps every channel
and briefly costs the station its link. Nothing that merely follows a link

sentinel instead of its value, at any depth and inside arrays, and so does the whole body when the
dot-path names one of those fields directly.

The sentinel is read-only: writing it back is refused at **422** rather
than stored, because storing it would destroy the credential.

of server strings for `time.ntp.servers`. Anything else is **422**.

UpdateConfig.description:
The operator's update document as micad saved it: the layer-2 keys and
nothing resolved.

A key the operator never set is **absent** and one they set to `null` is
**`null`**; both mean "take the baked default" and they are still two
different statements about the document. The resolved values — what this
device will actually dial and follow — are `GET /api/v1/update`'s
`lifecycle.policy` and `GET /api/v1/provisioning/status`'s `effective`.

UpdateConfigWrite.description:
The body of the update-configuration write: a **patch**, not a document.

A key this body omits is left exactly as it is on the device; a key set to
`null` clears an operator override so the baked default applies again; a
key with a value overrides it. That is what makes the write safe from a
console: a client that sent the whole resolved document back would pin the
image's defaults into the operator's layer and the device would stop
following its image, which nobody asked for.

Accepted keys: `policy` (`off`/`check`/`auto`), `checkIntervalMinutes`,
`checkAt` (`HH:MM` UTC, the time of day the check is anchored to),
`rebootPolicy` (`manual`/`window`), `channels` (the channel to follow for
each kind of set, as `{"core": "lts"}`: lowercase letters, digits and
hyphens; a kind named with `null` follows the image's again, a kind not
named is left as it is), `source.url`, `network`,
`maintenance` and `rebootGate`. Anything else — including a
trust anchor under any name, at any depth — is **422** naming the key: the
address this device dials is the operator's, what it will accept is baked
into the image, and no body may move that line.

UpdateState.description:
The update state document, verbatim from micad: `lifecycle` (state machine,
policy, reboot gate), per-slot status, `booted_slot`, `primary`,
`pending_not_confirmed`, `rollback`, `install` and `last_mark`.

`rollback` is the one place slot state is offered as a decision: micad's
`rollback_eligibility` resolves the alternate slot, says whether a manual
rollback is permitted, and names the refusal otherwise. There is no second
read route for it — this document is the single writer of that fact.

VlanParameters.description: The 802.1Q parameters of a VLAN interface.

parent.description:
Name of the `network` entry this VLAN sits on. A write naming a parent
it does not declare declares it with the entry that keeps the image's
configuration of that link, or is refused at 422.

WebConfiguration.description:
The `access.web` subtree as the device holds it.

Every field is required on a write: a `PUT` replaces the subtree.

httpPort.description:
TCP port of the HTTP listener. It serves the console, or only
redirects to HTTPS when that is enabled. Default 8080.

httpsEnabled.description: Whether apid serves HTTPS with its self-signed identity. Default off.

httpsPort.description: TCP port of the HTTPS listener. Default 8443.

mode.description:
Who reaches the API. `network`: the console and the API on the ports
below. `local`: only root on the device, through apid's local socket.
`off`: nobody; apid does not run. Leaving `network` from here needs
SSH on with an authorized key, the way back (`micad web network`).

WifiAccessPoint.description: The access point, as the device holds it.

address.description: The AP-side address in CIDR notation.

countryCode.description: The regulatory domain the radio is configured for.

oneOf.description:
The DHCP server clients get their addresses from. A read carries it
whenever `address` is valid; absent on a write is every address after
the access point's own and the server's default lease.

graceSeconds.description: Seconds it stays up after an uplink returns.

holdDownSeconds.description: Seconds without a usable uplink before the access point starts.

interface.description: The wireless interface it runs on.

psk.description:
The pre-shared key. **Read as `<redacted>`**; absent on a write keeps
the stored one, and absent on a device that never had one derives it
from the device credential.

security.description:
`wpa2-psk`, `wpa2-wpa3` (WPA3 beside WPA2, which needs a passphrase
rather than a raw PMK) or `open`; absent is `wpa2-psk`.

ssid.description: The advertised name; absent derives one from the device identity.

WifiApConfig.description:
The access point as the role write names it: `start` in place of `mode`,
which `enabled: false` turns off.

countryConfirmed.description: `true` confirms a `countryCode` other than the stored one.

start.description: `always`, or `provisioning`: only while no uplink works.

WifiCapabilities.description: What the radio can do as an access point.

acs.description: Whether the access point can choose its channel itself (channel 0).

apClientConcurrent.description: Whether the radio can be a station and an access point at once.

available.description:
Whether the device said; when not, the other members are what every
radio this image drives offers.

security.description:
The security types an access point can offer: `wpa2-psk`,
`wpa2-wpa3` where SAE and protected management frames run, `open`.

WifiChannels.description: The channels an access point may use in one country.

auto.description: Whether channel 0, the access point's own choice, is offered.

WifiClientConfig.description: The station's part of the role write.

addressing.description: The radio's own interface entry, replacing `network.<radio>`.

WifiClientRole.description:

Answers **404** when no stored network carries that SSID. There is no
The station role: the radio it runs on and whether it runs.

enabled.description: Whether the station role is started.

interface.description: The wireless interface it runs on.

WifiNetworkEntry.description:
One known WiFi network, in both directions.


`psk` differs by direction. On the way **in** it is the pre-shared key. On
the way **out** it is `"<redacted>"` whenever a key is stored. A body
carrying the sentinel back is refused at **422** rather than written.

autoConnect.description: Whether the station joins this network by itself; absent is true.

hidden.description: Whether the network hides its SSID.

psk.description:
The pre-shared key; absent for an open network, `"<redacted>"` on
every read of a network that has one.

ssid.description: The network name, which is also this entry's `DELETE` path segment.

enabled.description: Whether either role holds the radio.

locked.description: Whether another feature holds the Wi-Fi configuration; never, yet.

WifiRoleWrite.description: One write of the radio's role and the configuration of that role.

oneOf.description: The access point, required with `mode: ap` and refused otherwise.
The station's configuration, only with `mode: client`.

WireguardDefaults.description:
The values a new tunnel starts from: the first of each that nothing on the
device has. A value with no free candidate is absent.

address.description:
`10.2.0.1/24` … `10.254.0.1/24`, then `172.16.100.1/24` …
`172.16.255.1/24`: the first whose subnet overlaps no declared or
observed address, no peer's allowed IPs and no observed route other
than a default one.

listenPort.description: 51821 … 51899: the first no tunnel declares and no service holds.

name.description: `wg0`, `wg1`, … : the first no declared or observed link has.

udpPortsInUse.description:
The UDP ports services on the device hold, for a client choosing past
changes the device has not seen yet.

WireguardParameters.description:
The parameters of a WireGuard tunnel.

There is no private-key member and there never will be: this subtree is
served over `GET /api/v1/settings/network`, so a key in it is a key
published to every client. The private key lives in a mode-0640 file on the
device and only its public half is surfaced, through
`GET /api/v1/state/network` and the rotate action.

listenPort.description: UDP port to listen on; absent lets the kernel pick one.

peers.description:
The far ends of the tunnel. A `PUT` of this interface replaces them;
the peer collection route edits them one at a time.

WireguardPeerEntry.description: One far end of a WireGuard tunnel, in both directions.

endpoint.description: `host:port` to send to, for a peer this end initiates to.

name.description: A label for the peer, up to 64 characters with no control character.

persistentKeepalive.description: Keepalive interval in seconds, for a peer behind NAT.

presharedKey.description:
A pre-shared key: 32 bytes in padded base64. **Read as
`<redacted>`**; a `PUT` of the interface or the map that sends
`<redacted>` keeps the key stored for the peer with that public key.

publicKey.description:
The peer's X25519 public key: 32 bytes in padded base64. It is also
this entry's `DELETE` path segment, and its alphabet contains `/`, so a
key carrying one is percent-encoded there.

WireguardPeerState.description:
One peer as the peer collection reads it: whether it has a pre-shared key
rather than the key, and room for what the tunnel reports about it.

latestHandshake.description:
The last handshake, Unix seconds, as the kernel reports it; `null`
when the peer never completed one or the tunnel could not be asked.

presharedKey.description: Whether a pre-shared key is stored for the peer; the key is never read.

publicKey.description: The peer's X25519 public key, also its `DELETE` path segment.

rxBytes.description:
Bytes received from the peer; `null` when the tunnel could not be
asked.

txBytes.description: Bytes sent to the peer; `null` when the tunnel could not be asked.

WireguardRotation.description:
The body of a successful key rotation: the public half, and nothing else.

There is no `privateKey` member here and there will not be one. The private
half never leaves micad — there is no read-back route for the private key,
ever; not redacted-on-read, nonexistent — so this struct is the whole of
what a rotation can answer.

publicKey.description: The new base64 X25519 public key, which is what the far end needs.
